catalog_quote: The basic foot type in Limilngan is the trochee. In general, polysyllabic morphemes constitute independent stress domains and feet are aligned from the left edge of these morphologically determined domains. Monosyllabic or consonantal suffixes are incorporated into the preceding domain. ... Consequently, all disyllabic words have an initial stress, regardless of their internal morphological structure. [p.32] The majority of trisyllabic uninflected words also bear stress on their first syllable. The other trisyllables bear stress on the second syllable. The appearance of penultimate stress in trisyllables is not random, but rather shows a relationship to syllable weight. Trisyllables with a heavy second syllable are likely to show penultimate stress. As vowel length is not contrastive in Limilngan, syllable weight depends solely on the nature of the coda. [p.34] Quadrisyllabic words generally have a secondary stress on the first syllable, and a primary stress on the third syllable. [p.35] The general pattern of stress placement in verbal words is that the first syllable of the verb root bears a stress, and that thereafter each alternate syllable also bears a stress, subject to the proviso that final syllables do not bear a stress. The final stress is the primary stress. [p.36] Stress placement in verbs is affected by considerations of syllable weight. Syllables closed by coda clusters, continuants, taps, laterals, and hetero-organic nasals attract stress.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Trochaic feet built left-to-right from the left edge of each polysyllabic morpheme (the stress domain); monosyllabic/consonantal suffixes join the preceding domain; final syllables are not stressed; where a word has several stresses the LAST (rightmost) stress is primary (verbs p.35: 'The final stress is the primary stress'; quadrisyllabic nouns: secondary on 1st, primary on 3rd). Default outcome: initial stress in disyllables and most trisyllables; but heavy syllables (coda clusters, and codas that are laterals, taps, continuants or hetero-organic nasals — not homorganic nasals, geminate halves or most stop codas; vowel length is not contrastive) attract stress, giving penultimate stress in trisyllables with a heavy 2nd syllable; comparative vowel sonority is a further, weaker factor. Monosyllabic prefix complexes are unstressed before polysyllabic roots but stressed before monosyllabic roots; polysyllabic prefix complexes take a secondary stress on their first syllable. A few verb paradigms ('get', 'give', 'hit') have irregular stress on the pre-root syllable.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Explicitly described: perceptible primary vs secondary distinction (primary = greatest amplitude); alternate syllables after the first stressed syllable of the root carry stress; polysyllabic prefix complexes carry secondary stress on their initial syllable; in quadrisyllables secondary on 1st syllable, primary on 3rd; words with three stresses are common but no secondary/tertiary ranking among non-primary stresses.
new_statements.exceptions: Trisyllables with heavy (cluster/sonorant-coda) 2nd syllable take penult stress (8 of 9 with coda clusters; 4 of 4 with lateral/tap/continuant coda; 4 of 7 with hetero-organic nasal coda; only 2 of 12 with hetero-organic stop coda); eight open-syllable trisyllables with unexplained penult stress (e.g. uwagi 'fire', luwarli 'rat'), possibly vowel sonority; quadrisyllables 'less predictable'; irregular pre-root stress in paradigms of 'get' and disyllabic-prefix + monosyllabic-verb words ('give', 'hit'); word-level suffixes and reduplication/compounds form their own stress domains (2.6.3-2.6.4).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress, described over morphologically defined domains (root+root-level suffixes vs prefixes vs word-level suffixes); based on the speech of the last fluent speaker (Felix Holmes); amplitude is the main perceptual cue, vowel length uncertain, tone stated to be phrase-level not word-level (5.1, Appendix A). Author compares the system to Larrakia's quantity-sensitive trochees with final-foot primary stress, noting Limilngan's coda-sonorancy sensitivity is less consistent.
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes Limilngan proper (glottocode nucl1327 'Nuclear Limilngan', ISO lmc), recorded from the last fluent speaker Felix Holmes in the Mary River region; not Wulna. No dialect differentiation described.

new_statements.relation_note: Same work as the existing weight-sensitive statement (section 2.6).35 rule, and adds the secondary-stress inventory, the weight condition on verbs, the listed irregular paradigms, and the p.32 statement that 'tone is fundamentally phrase-level and not word-level in scope (5.1, Appendix A). Consequently, tone is not a reliable indicator of word-level stress.' The catalog record itself has an empty rule field, so this fills it. Appendix A is a text collection with no intonation section; the 'Appendix A (intonation)' label on the work entry only reflects Harvey's cross-reference for phrase-level tone.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Trochaic feet built from the left edge of each polysyllabic morpheme (root plus root-level suffixes form one domain; prefixes do not). All disyllables are initial-stressed. Trisyllabic nouns are mostly initial-stressed but take penultimate stress when the second syllable is heavy (coda cluster, or a lateral/tap/continuant/hetero-organic nasal coda); quadrisyllables have secondary stress on syllable 1 and primary on syllable 3. In verbs the first syllable of the verb root is stressed, then every other syllable, never the final syllable; the last (rightmost) stress is primary; a polysyllabic prefix complex takes a secondary stress on its first syllable, a monosyllabic one is unstressed. Weight (closed syllables of the listed kinds) attracts stress in verbs too. Stress is cued mainly by amplitude; tone is phrase-level and not a word-stress cue.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Explicitly distinguished: 'There is a perceptible difference in Limilngan between primary and secondary stress' (p.32); words with three stresses are common in verbs, one primary and the others not ranked further. Quadrisyllables: secondary on syllable 1, primary on syllable 3 (p.34). Polysyllabic prefix complexes: secondary on their initial syllable (p.35); a monosyllabic prefix complex gets a secondary stress only when the verb root's first syllable is unstressed (p.36). Disyllabic word-level suffixes bear a secondary stress on their first syllable; =lilkgami stressed on syllable 1, =nijilni on syllable 2 (p.38); in the sequence =wany=mirl, =wany carries a secondary stress (p.39). Appendix D marks primary (acute) and secondary (grave) on every verbal form.
new_statements.exceptions: Eight trisyllables with an open second syllable nonetheless have penultimate stress (p.34, e.g. uwagi 'fire', dinngagi 'already'), possibly vowel-sonority effects; stress in quadrisyllables is 'evidently less predictable than that in trisyllables' (p.35). The 'get' paradigm places stress irregularly on the syllable before the root (Past Perfective, Irrealis; p.36). In verbal words with a disyllabic prefix complex and a monosyllabic verb, the vowel of the Future or Irrealis prefix bears the stress (pp.36-37). A few paradigms are stressed as if monomorphemic, e.g. 'to get up' (Appendix D) and the body-part noun -inan 'nose' (Appendix B) (p.37). The suffix -ini 'Another' attracts stress whereas verbal -iji 'here' does not (p.37); one problematic -ngan form (3-60) (p.38). Monosyllabic word-level suffixes (=ji, =mirl, =wany) are unstressed and do not join the stem's domain (p.38). Word-level compounding reduplication gives each half its own primary stress (p.40).
new_statements.identity_note: The description is of the Limilngan language proper (Harvey's own fieldwork on Felix Holmes's speech; Appendix A texts were recorded by Frances Morphy in 1983-84 and checked with Lena Henry in 2000). No other variety is described; the note that Wanyjuwanyjuwa has Giimbiyu and Gaagudju name variants concerns text content, not phonology.
